newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala peace talks face worst crisis yet.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala peace talks face worst crisis yet.

text.p: Marathon talks between Guatemala's government and leftist rebels to end Central America's longest civil war have stalled in the home stretch over a kidnapping allegedly carried out by a rebel commander.

The talks have been in abeyance since Oct. 28, when the government accused the rebels of violating terms of the negotiations after the kidnapping of a wealthy 86-year-old woman. The crisis interrupted talks that had dragged on for six years, halting the countdown to a scheduled December signing of a final peace accord after 36 years of war.

"I believe this crisis is the worst we have had because it comes toward the end of the negotiations," Hector Rosada, a sociologist who led the government team of peace negotiators for three years in the early 1990s, said.
Rigoberta Menchu, the Guatemalan Indian activist who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992, has also called this the most serious crisis to hit the often rocky peace talks.

Rosada and Menchu, church and human rights groups and leftist members of congress have all urged the government to continue talks for the sake of the people of Guatemala, more than 100,000 of whom died during the brutal civil war.

Olga Alvarado de Novella, a member of one of Guatemala's wealthiest families, was kidnapped on Aug. 25 and released more than a month later after officials arrested rebel commander Rafael Valdizon and charged him with the kidnapping.

Leaders of the rebel Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) exiled in Mexico City last week acknowledged that Valdizon, whom it called an "ex-commander," had taken part in the kidnapping. It condemned his action and said it occurreed without the knowledge of the group's command.
The URNG offered another olive branch on Monday, announcing it would also halt armed propaganda activities and offering to sign a bilateral cease-fire before continuing with talks.
Both sides want to avoid a collapse of peace talks and could meet this weekend in a bid to get the derailed process back on track, a diplomat close to the process said.

Analysts said a peace accord was in the interests of both sides. The URNG does not enjoy much popular support and the government has been under international pressure to clean up its dismal human rights record.
Mostly Indian peasants have suffered during the civil war, which peaked in the early 1980s when the army mounted a brutal counter-insurgency campaign in rural areas.

Both sides met directly for the first time in Oslo in 1991 and signed a democratic accord but the process then stalled for more than two years. Peace was endangered by pressure from right wing groups who discouraged the talks and by a new wave of human rights abuses, including a number of political assassinations in the capital.
But President Alvaro Arzu, a businessman who wants to improve the economy by ending the war, pushed firmly for talks and this is the first year negotiations have gone smoothly.

The URNG announced a unilateral cease-fire in May and Arzu responded by ordering the army to halt all counterinsurgency activities. In September negotiators signed a historic accord reducing the army by one third and limiting its postwar role.
